title: Tamsin and the Visitor
premise: Tamsin Kavanagh, a rationalist property surveyor, is sent to appraise Hollowmere House and finds her childhood imaginary friend, Wren, waiting on the porch — unchanged after thirty years. The house 'appraises back,' cataloguing its inhabitants and counting down toward a reckoning that consumes whoever remains when the count completes. As Tamsin uncovers that the house feeds on belonging — trading memory for survival — she must convince the trapped family to abandon everything they remember in order to escape. In the end Tamsin pays the price herself: she gives up her own memories of home so the family can leave, walking out of Hollowmere a stranger to her own past, while Wren stays behind as the new keeper of the count.
about_author: Silas Winterbourne is the pen name of a former rural assessor who spent a decade appraising derelict properties across the English moors and never fully explained why he stopped. He writes horror from a farmhouse he refuses to name, claiming some houses prefer to remain off the record.

chapters.title: The Commission
chapters.summary: Tamsin accepts an unusually lucrative appraisal of Hollowmere House despite its reputation for failed sales. Her POV establishes her hard-edged skepticism and a vague ache of homesickness she can't source. The emotional beat: professional confidence masking a hollow place inside.

chapters.title: Hollowmere
chapters.summary: Tamsin arrives at the house, which seems subtly larger inside than out. Measurements refuse to reconcile; her instruments drift. A child's chalk hopscotch grid on the porch counts down from nine. Beat: unease sharpening into denial.

chapters.title: Wren
chapters.summary: On the porch sits Wren, Tamsin's childhood imaginary friend, ageless and patient. Tamsin's rational mind scrambles for explanations — coincidence, a lookalike, stress. Wren only says, 'You came back. It noticed.' Beat: the collapse of her certainty begins.

chapters.title: The Family
chapters.summary: Tamsin meets the Aldous family — parents Edith and Marcus, teenage twins — who seem oddly placid, their memories of moving in suspiciously smooth. POV shifts briefly to Edith, who cannot recall her mother's face. Beat: dread through small absences.

chapters.title: Appraisal Back
chapters.summary: Tamsin's survey notes rewrite themselves overnight, describing not the house but her: losses, fears, the year she stopped believing. She realizes the house is valuing her the way she values properties. Beat: violation and vertigo.

chapters.title: Nine Rooms
chapters.summary: Wren explains the rules: the house holds nine rooms but only eight souls may remain when the count reaches zero; the surplus is 'kept.' Tamsin refuses to believe until she finds a sealed room containing a previous surveyor's badge. Beat: belief arrives as horror.

chapters.title: What Edith Gave
chapters.summary: Edith confesses that when money ran out, the house offered them security in exchange for memories — one per month. The twins have already forgotten their grandmother. Tamsin sees her own future in them. Beat: pity curdling into urgency.

chapters.title: The Count
chapters.summary: The porch chalk now reads four. Rooms begin rearranging; exits lead back to the hall. Tamsin maps the house obsessively, her surveyor's discipline the only weapon she has. Beat: determination against encroaching claustrophobia.

chapters.title: Marcus's Bargain
chapters.summary: Marcus has been secretly trading memories to keep the family comfortable, spending himself hollow. He no longer remembers why he loves his wife. Tamsin confronts him; he thanks her blankly. Beat: grief for a man still breathing.

chapters.title: Wren's History
chapters.summary: Wren reveals it was once a real child kept by the house generations ago, made into a 'friend' to lure believers and skeptics alike. Tamsin realizes she was chosen, not visited. Beat: betrayal by the one figure she trusted as a child.

chapters.title: Three
chapters.summary: Count at three. The twins begin sleepwalking to the sealed room, drawn by something that calls them by name. Tamsin physically drags them back and decides escape must happen before zero, not after. Beat: protective fury.

chapters.title: The Previous Surveyor
chapters.summary: In the cellar Tamsin finds the last appraiser's notes: he learned the exit exists only where the house cannot see itself — a blind spot in its own appraisal. His notes end mid-sentence. Beat: hope with a body count attached.

chapters.title: Edith Refuses
chapters.summary: When Tamsin proposes leaving, Edith resists — the house has taken so much that leaving means admitting nothing is left to return to. Family fractures over the kitchen table as walls visibly creep closer. Beat: the price of belonging made explicit.

chapters.title: Two
chapters.summary: Count at two. The house offers Tamsin her own deal: stay, and it will restore every memory she's ever lost, including whatever made her stop believing. She nearly says yes. Beat: temptation rendered intimate.

chapters.title: The Blind Spot
chapters.summary: Tamsin deduces the blind spot: the room the house cannot value — the one space it never measured, her own childhood bedroom doorway, where Wren first appeared. Belief, it turns out, is the one asset the house can't appraise. Beat: intellectual triumph, fragile.

chapters.title: One
chapters.summary: Count at one. The house fights back, flooding them with fabricated memories of lives they never lived elsewhere, making outside feel like the lie. Marcus, nearly empty, wanders toward the sealed room. Beat: reality itself becomes untrustworthy.

chapters.title: Marcus Stays
chapters.summary: Too spent to leave, Marcus chooses to remain, asking only that Edith not watch him be 'kept.' The house seals him into the ninth room gently, almost kindly. Beat: devastating cost of what he traded away.

chapters.title: Zero Hour
chapters.summary: Count at zero. With the family short one soul, the count resets — and the house turns fully on Tamsin, the surplus. Wren stands between her and the sealed room, duty-bound and weeping. Beat: climax opens.

chapters.title: The Appraisal of Tamsin Kavanagh
chapters.summary: The house presents its final valuation: Tamsin's entire history, itemized. To pass through the blind spot she must surrender what she values most — her memories of home, of belonging anywhere. She signs herself away. Beat: sacrifice as climax.

chapters.title: Out
chapters.summary: Tamsin leads Edith and the twins through the unmeasured doorway into grey morning light. They are free and hollowed; she does not know their names, or her own address, or why she is crying. Beat: escape without victory.

chapters.title: The New Keeper
chapters.summary: Inside, Wren takes up the chalk and begins a fresh count, becoming what it once suffered under. The house settles, satisfied, already drafting letters to new buyers. Beat: cyclical dread, quiet and cold.

chapters.title: A Stranger at the Gate
chapters.summary: Months later, Tamsin — living on instinct and a notebook of facts about herself — receives a commission to appraise a house called Hollowmere. On the porch, a figure waits, unchanged. She doesn't believe. Not yet. Beat: the loop reopens, ending on held breath.
